findings.title: hash01 has no final mix, so algorithmic events are all-or-nothing per world: 44% of worlds never get one, 27% get 20 or more
findings.where: js/rng.js:7 (root cause); js/engine.js:463-466 (_algoEvent); js/session.js:972 (shockStart)
findings.scenario: _algoEvent rolls hash01(worldSeed + 'algo' + day) <= 0.14 for each of days 4..86, meant as 83 independent 14% draws (about 11.6 events a run, sd about 3.2). hash() is FNV-1a, whose last step is a multiply with no avalanche, so keys that differ only in their trailing characters (the day number) give values that creep by about 0.004 a day. The 83 rolls are one slow ramp: a world whose ramp sits above 0.14 never gets an event, one that sits near it gets a long run of consecutive event days. The kind and class picks (seed+'k'+day, seed+'c'+day) ramp the same way, so the same event on the same asset class repeats on consecutive days. It is on by default (env.algo true, session.js:116; the dashboard toggle ships checked) in both classrooms (world seed = 4-letter room code) and Quick play (seed 'solo-NNNNNN'). Measured over 20,000 room codes and 20,000 solo seeds: mean 11.9 events per run (as designed) but sd 15.6 (designed 3.2); 43% of rooms and 44% of solo runs have no algorithmic event in 90 days; 28% and 27% have 20 or more; the same event on the same class on consecutive days about 6 times a run; up to 63 event days. In a real Game, room GWQX gets 35 (viral Used Commuter Sedan then viral Barn-Find Roadster on days 20-27 in a row, a 2.5x demand multiplier renewed daily) and room KMQD gets none, while FACULTY_KIT.md:58 and BALANCE.md:184 sell these as surprise events every student sees. Session.shockStart (session.js:972) uses the same hash, so the gradebook agrees with the engine and shares the flaw. The same flaw makes the herd's 12-hour noise (cohort.js:28, lag-1 autocorrelation 0.89) a slow drift and the Second-Chance warning draw (engine.js:556, lag-1 0.88; that perk's balance is a known item and is not re-reported). js/meta/progress.js:14-16 (Progress.unit) already documents this exact weakness and carries the finalizer, but the shared hash01 does not use it. Keys whose varying part is not last (deal.js lead-id quirk, checked on 2,264 real lead ids) are fine.

findings.title: Selling the starting paperclip for less than the cheapest lot strands the founder for the whole run: every pool sale for most Backgrounds, 43% of day-1 buyers, with no warning and no way back
findings.where: js/engine.js:878 (sellPool) and js/engine.js:663 (pitch, cash at :696); js/meta/quests.js:35 (q01a); js/ui/drawers/stock.js:151 and :157 (empty state, poolConfirm)
findings.scenario: Everyone starts with $0 and one paperclip. If the founder turns the paperclip into cash and gets less than the cheapest lot on the shelf, nothing in the game can put a crate or a cent in their hands again: the bank opens at $1,000 net worth, no manager can be hired, there is nothing to pitch, quests and levels pay XP and points only, and the cheapest lot posted in 90 days was $0.05 (the paperclip lot) against $0.0441 in hand. The run idles to day 90 at net worth $0.04 (EEI about 4e-5). Stock > 'Sell to the pool' on the lone crate strands the founder in 40 of 40 seeds for 9 of the 13 build configurations (no Background, connected, grad, veteran, heir, roots, native, second, pro), 39 of 40 for creator and about half the seeds for trades, immigrant and gigger; the confirm dialog (stock.js:157) only says 'You get about $0.04', and after the sale the Stock empty state says 'Buy your first lot in the Market' with $0.04. Pitching to a non-urgent cash buyer strands too (a scrapper pays $0.023 against a $0.05 lot): 640 of the 1,500 day-1 buyer options over 300 seeds (43%). The first quest, q01a 'First Swap', reads 'Trade your paperclip to a buyer in The Scrap Yard. Any buyer who bites counts.' and pays 50 XP for the stranding sale. What does protect a novice: the Market lists the guaranteed urgent buyer first and the first-listed buyer who bites never strands (0 of 400 seeds), the best-paying buyer never strands (0 of 400), and barter buyers hand goods back. So the trap is any off-path first move, including the one-click pool sale. A random first-five-days player ends stranded 64% of the time (300 starts).

findings.fixSketch: Options for the author. (a) Engine guard, covers API and Deal Room callers: in pitch and sellPool refuse a sale that would leave no crate, no manager, no freight, no escrow, no unsettled proceeds and less cash than the cheapest posted lot in every open district, with a plain message ('That sale would leave you $0.04 and nothing to sell; the cheapest lot here costs $0.05'); barter results that return goods are exempt. (b) Rescue instead of refusal: when that stranded state holds at an hourly tick, hand back one paperclip crate once a day ('you found a paperclip'), noted in news and ledger, so the run is always recoverable. (c) Teaching only: warn in poolConfirm and in the Market quote when the founder holds one crate and the payout is below the cheapest lot, and reword q01a to 'a buyer who gives you something to climb on'. (c) alone leaves the trap open for any non-UI caller; (a) or (b) closes it. Whichever is chosen, keep the barter ladder and the urgent-buyer lesson intact.
findings.testSketch: For seeds 1..60 and each of the 12 Backgrounds: call sellPool on the starting clip and, separately, pitch it to every day-1 lead; assert each outcome is either ok:false with a message, or leaves a way forward (some posted lot costs <= cash + any circle room, or a crate/rescue exists within 24 virtual hours). Assert q01a still completes through the urgent buyer.

findings.title: Fees and taxes have no ceiling: friction 3.0x plus stacked Credit Crunches make a sale cost more than it pays (negative pool proceeds, pool refilled above its cap)
findings.where: js/engine.js:289-293 (instFee, zoneTax), :867-893 (poolQuote, sellPool), :638 (quotePitch), :249 and :449 (mods sums fees; injectEvent replace skips started copies)
findings.scenario: instFee = (0.025 + sum of live event fees) x Fintech x friction x perk and zoneTax = tax x friction, with no cap. The dashboard allows friction up to 3.0, and 'Credit Crunch' (fed: +0.095 fee for 360 hours) can be pressed again an hour after the last press: the 'Replace the scheduled copy (pull it forward instead of stacking)' option only drops copies that have not started (engine.js:449), so a started crunch stays and mods() adds the second one's fee (engine.js:249). At friction 3.0 with three live crunches the pool haircut is 103% (district-1 friction 0.1 + instFee 0.93) and a district-12 pitch pays 35% tax + 93% fee = 128% of the price. Effects: poolQuote total -$0.63 and the message 'Sold for $-0.63.'; cash falls and s.pool[1] rises to 5000.63 against a cap of 5000 (invariant broken); the ledger row carries amt -0.63; a $26,336 pitch in district 12 cost the seller $7,361 and logged 'Traded, no gain.'. Two crunches at 3.0x already reach 80% / 99%; two at 2.0x reach 53% / 66%. Only the instructor can reach it, but the UI offers no hint that the combination is destructive, and the engine should not let a sale net negative.

findings.title: A hand sale resets lastAuto, so the instructor's 'Operational bottlenecks' panel never flags a founder who stopped every manager but still sells by hand
findings.where: js/engine.js:689 (pitch sets s.lastAuto); js/engine.js:1127 (cycle) and :1844 (published as lastAutoHour); js/cohort.js:178; js/ui/instructor.js:122 and :171
findings.scenario: s.lastAuto is meant to be the last automated pipeline cycle: the panel footer says 'No automated asset velocity for more than 3 virtual days: a pipeline-management breakdown', docs/FACULTY_KIT.md:60 says 'pipelines have shown no automated activity for more than three virtual days', and tests/cohort.test.mjs:162 says 'only the one who has not automated for three days is static'. But Game.pitch also sets s.lastAuto = s.hour on every completed hand sale (engine.js:689), and publicSnapshot publishes it as lastAutoHour. A founder past Metro Hub who pauses or never hires managers and sells one crate a day by hand therefore never shows as static, which is exactly the student the rubric row 'Working capital and pipeline velocity' wants the instructor to find. In the repro a founder with 17 paused managers is flagged 'static' on pause-day 4 when they do nothing, and never flagged when they make one hand pitch a day.

(3) Publish both lastAutoHour and lastSaleHour and show two columns. (1) matches the stated intent.

findings.title: A throwing event listener leaves the day tick half done: profit counted twice, a missing history row, checkpoint and algorithmic-event roll, and the same hour's audits skipped
findings.where: js/engine.js:118-124 (emit calls this.onEvent unguarded) and :1345 (emit('day') mid-tick); js/ui/shell.js:300-306; js/session.js:590
findings.scenario: Game.emit calls the UI's onEvent with no guard. _dayTick emits 'day' after pushing dp but before the hist row, acc.profit reset, niche trim, next day's _algoEvent roll and the day checkpoint. The shell's handler (shell.js:300-306) calls progress.onEvent and cues?.event bare; only ctx.emit is wrapped (shell.js:56). If either throws on a 'day' event, stepHour leaves the hour advanced but the tail of the tick undone, the same hour's _audits/_marginCall are skipped, and Session.tick (session.js:590) does not catch, so the next tick carries on from the corrupted state: realized profit is booked in two days of dp (the exit premium averages dp), the day's hist row and checkpoint never exist (a later rewind lands a day earlier), and that student never rolls the day's algorithmic event while the rest of the room does, so the shared seed no longer replays identically across clients. No listener in the tree throws today (the real Progress attached to 12 chaos seeds for 1,800 hours: 0 throws), so this is hardening, but one UI bug in a three-listener chain silently desynchronizes a run.
findings.repro: cd /tmp/audit-scratch/engine-core && node listener.mjs printed: 'no listener error                  hour 48 | dp [250,0] | acc.profit 0 | hist rows 2 | checkpoints 0,1,2' / 'listener threw at the day-2 tick   hour 48 | dp [250,250] | acc.profit 0 | hist rows 1 | checkpoints 0,2' / 'thrown out of advanceTo: listener bug'. node progress_attach.mjs 1-12 1800 (real Progress on chaos games) printed 'distinct problems 0'.
findings.fixSketch: Wrap the listener call in Game.emit (try { this.onEvent?.(evt) } catch (e) { console.error(e) }) so an observer can never break the simulation, and wrap progress.onEvent and cues?.event in shell.js the way ctx.emit is wrapped. Optionally move emit('day') to the end of _dayTick.
findings.testSketch: Game with an onEvent that throws once on the first 'day' event: advanceTo(48) must not throw and must end with the same dp, hist length, checkpoint keys and events list as a game with no listener.

findings.title: The Veteran's 'macro shocks hit 40% softer' also mutes booms and the algorithmic events
findings.where: js/engine.js:257-262 (mods); js/data/perks.js:26-27; js/ui/draft.js:55
findings.scenario: The perk text promises that macro shocks 'hit 40% softer' and the draft scores it as 'risk cover'. mods() scales every live effect toward neutral, whatever its direction: mult = 1 + (mult - 1) x 0.6 for demand, price and speed, and the fee, rate, overhead, repair and international terms. It also applies to the three algorithmic events and instructor-injected ones, which the text does not call macro. A Veteran who reads the TikTok warning and stocks up earns less than a neutral player who does the same. Whether a perk should mute upside is a design call; the code and the text currently disagree.

findings.title: acceptOffer keeps no record of accepted offers: a repeated call pays again and mints another copy of the proposer's crates
findings.where: js/engine.js:1693-1735 (acceptOffer); js/session.js:759 and :822-834 (the only caller)
findings.scenario: acceptOffer validates the offer and then moves cash and crates, but never records the offer id, so calling it again with the same offer pays the cash or crates again and creates a fresh copy of the offered crates (new 'A' ids), while the proposer's escrow settles once (finalizeOffer deletes it). In the repro A offers one bike for its fair price and B accepts three times: all three return ok; B ends with 3 bikes, A with none; the pair holds 3 bikes instead of 1 and $42.16 less cash (B paid three times, A once). With an in-band lopsided offer (a $100 bike for $60) each replay would mint $40. This is not reachable from the shipped flow: Session moves the offer from incoming to accepting at acceptIncoming and deletes accepting before calling acceptOffer in _onConfirm, and the Practice Partner path uses finalizeOffer only. It is an engine-level breach of 'goods conserved' that depends on every caller being perfect, in a client a student can drive from the console; the same repeat would also push a second royalty stream for one offer id.

reports.coverage: Read in full: js/deal.js, js/play/{haggle,inspect,pitch,repair,auction}.js, js/ui/deal.js, js/rng.js, plus the engine paths they call (quotePitch, pitch, buyLot, repair, recordInspect, _spawnLot, xp, rewindTo), session save/rewind, identity, the Menu save export, js/audio/wire.js (hidden-field reads) and the tests that hold this area (deal, ui-deal, the `tried` tests, play-*). Ran about 35 Node scripts: a hostile-action fuzz of all five games (1,294 actions, frozen inputs, JSON round trips), about 3,600 hostile or extreme parameter sets, 723 random UI sessions (3,201 clicks on only the enabled buttons, world changed mid-deal), 20,000-deal Quick par checks, calibration and balance sweeps, a 6,134-string text scan; and 6 headless Chrome scripts with real mouse and keyboard events. The five games held their contract (no throws, no mutation, finite numbers, bounds [0.6,1.4] / [0.85,1.15] / [0.9,1.3], deterministic, JSON-stable); the pure modules have no clock, randomness or DOM; sound never reads a hidden field; `first move final` held against reload (pagehide saves), Quick-after-a-peek and reopening for Close, Bid and Fix; no double-buy, double-sell or buy-after-removal reached. findings.title: The XP on a walk-away card (and quest/achievement progress) is computed from a passed lot's hidden truth, so Read tells you for free what the lot was
findings.where: js/engine.js:768-770 (recordInspect, called from js/deal.js:484); shown at js/ui/deal.js:242; score defined at js/play/inspect.js:114-115
findings.scenario: Read a lot, conclude, press Pass. The lot stays on the shelf and the card says No deal, but conclude() has already called recordInspect, which pays Read XP = 8 + 22 x score (engine.js:768). score = 1 - 0.6*min(1,|estimate-truth|/0.25) - 0.4*p for a genuine lot, 1 - 0.2*qe - 0.8*(1-p) for a fake (inspect.js:114-115). The card prints '+N XP', so N gives |estimate - true quality| to about +-0.01 (the truth is estimate +- that, and the other side is often outside the 0.7-1.15 range). For a lot the player did NOT suspect (p small) the score ranges of a fake and of a genuine lot do not overlap, so N also says which it is: of 149 unsuspected counterfeits the XP flags 65 as fake with certainty, never calls one genuine (0 of 149), and certifies 360 of 364 genuine lots as genuine. A player reads, passes, looks at the XP, and comes back to buy only the certified-genuine lots; due diligence stops costing anything. The same call emits inspect {score, fake, caught}, so quest 'Spot the Fake' (q04b), 'Counterfeit Cop', 'Good Eye' and the daily score bounties move for a lot that is still hidden. The author closed the card's other numbers for exactly this reason (deal.js:596-598, 610 hide net, reveal and the haggle lesson on a walk); XP is the door left open.

Pick a pair, read the verdict (+0.12 fit, buyer is x1.07 as keen, the buyer's own words), press Leave: nothing is marked, the buyer stays, and the same table opens with a fresh Pitch. Ten sittings show all ten pairs and the 11th plays the best (score 1.00, XP for a perfect pitch). The repo treats this as normal: remaining-engine.test.mjs sits ten fresh sittings at one buyer, and a comment in meta-academy.test.mjs describes leaving before the Close and tapping the buyer again as the way out of a cool pitch. findings.title: The reduced-motion slider (a free setting) beats real human timing at every Ops level, so the dial's skill is optional

Read .github/workflows/pages.yml, scripts/stage.mjs, index.html, 404.html and the relevant tests (tests/remaining-engine.test.mjs, tests/multiplayer.test.mjs) to see what is already held and avoid re-reporting it. Did not get to: fuzzing permessage-deflate / compression-specific framing, IPv6/dual-stack binding of static.mjs's HOST=0.0.0.0, or a from-the-browser (headless Chrome) reproduction of the relay findings (they are all server-side and were fully reproducible over raw WebSocket/TCP, which is a stronger proof than driving a browser). One other process was briefly found writing files into this same scratch directory (e1-starve.mjs/e2-squat.mjs, not authored by me); I isolated my own scripts into a `dyn/` subdirectory and every finding below is backed only by output from calls in this transcript, not by those files.

findings.title: A room's owner-recovery token can never bind once any no-token instructor-role connection claims the seat first — not a race that is sometimes lost, but a deterministic, permanent lock-out
findings.where: server/relay.mjs:82-90 (claim)
findings.scenario: claim() only sets room.ownerProof when `!seat || seat.pid === ws.pid`. The very first instructor-role connection to a fresh/forgotten room that brings NO token (a stray tab with role=instructor and no `owner` param, a second device that hasn't loaded localStorage yet, a classmate who flips the URL's role param out of curiosity, or an attacker) takes the seat via the `!seat` branch without ever setting room.ownerProof. From then on room.ownerProof stays null forever: the real instructor's later connections, however many, with the exact correct 32-char owner token, can never satisfy `(room.ownerProof == null && (!seat || seat.pid === ws.pid))` (seat.pid is the squatter's pid, not theirs), so the token never binds and the instructor can never reclaim the seat for the life of the room. This directly contradicts the file's own header comment ("the room's owner token... a secret the instructor keeps a copy of") and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md/docs/FACULTY_KIT.md's entire 'take back a room' story, which both promise the token always wins. It is also the practical outcome of the ordinary scenario the docs explicitly cite: a relay restart (Render/Fly/campus VM redeploy) or a room forgotten after EMPTY_MS both reset `room` to a fresh object, so whichever instructor-role connection reaches the new object first permanently decides whether the token will ever work again.
findings.repro:
node /tmp/audit-scratch/relay-and-static-server-security/dyn/seat-claim-bug.mjs against the unmodified server/relay.mjs (createRelay() from the worktree, no CLI, no mocking). Printed:
`after student joins: room.ownerProof = null room.seat = null room.owner = null`
`after a no-token instructor connects: room.ownerProof = null room.seat = PC-OTHER room.owner = PC-OTHER`
`attempt 0: real instructor with the CORRECT owner token connects -> room.ownerProof = null, room.seat = PC-OTHER, became seat holder: false` (repeated for attempt 1 and 2, three separate reconnect attempts, all false)
`student heard a clock from: []` -- the real instructor's clock message never reached the student at all.
A second script (seat-race.mjs) reproduces the same outcome end-to-end over real WebSocket reconnects after (a) killing and restarting the relay process and (b) letting the room sit empty past EMPTY_MS: in both cases the student only ever hears clock/inject messages `from:"PC-EVIL"`, including a fake `hour:999` and an injected 'crash' shock, even after the real instructor reconnects with the correct token on a brand-new Founder ID (the exact 'take back a room' flow docs/FACULTY_KIT.md describes).
findings.fixSketch: Bind the token independent of current seat state: the first valid token presented for a room with room.ownerProof still null should always bind, e.g. `if (ownerProof) { if (room.ownerProof == null) room.ownerProof = ownerProof; if (sameHash(room.ownerProof, ownerProof)) { room.owner = ws.pid; room.seat = { pid: ws.pid, ws, left: 0 }; return; } }` (drop the `(!seat || seat.pid === ws.pid)` guard on the binding line only; the sameHash branch already correctly reclaims the seat from whoever holds it).
findings.testSketch: Unit test against createRelay(): connect a student, then a no-token instructor (asserts it takes the seat, as today), then a real instructor with a token minted at room creation; assert room.ownerProof is set to that token's hash and room.seat.pid is the real instructor's pid. Add this alongside tests/remaining-engine.test.mjs's existing 'Relay owner' test, which only covers the token-already-bound case and so does not catch this.

findings.title: 800 connect-snapshot-and-leave sockets (about 2.5 seconds of one script) permanently fill a room's pid table and lock out every future real student for the rest of the class
findings.where: server/relay.mjs:92-97 (pruneKeys), 130-135 (connection handler)
findings.scenario: pruneKeys() only considers evicting a pid when `!k.snapped`. An attacker who knows the room code opens ~800 short-lived connections, each sending one valid `snap` message (satisfying the explicit 20 msg/s rate limit easily) before disconnecting. Every one of those pids is marked `snapped: true` and can never be pruned again, no matter how long ago it left (the `at - k.left > GHOST_MS` check is never reached because `!k.snapped` already fails first). Once `room.keys.size >= MAX_ROOM * 2` (800), every brand-new real student is refused with 1013 'room full' -- forever, as long as the instructor (or anyone) keeps the room's `clients` set non-empty, since the whole-room eviction (EMPTY_MS) only fires when clients.size reaches 0.
findings.repro:
node /tmp/audit-scratch/relay-and-static-server-security/dyn/keytable-lockout.mjs against the unmodified relay. Printed:
`attack took 2450 ms; instructor is the only one connected now`
`real new students: [ 'opened 1013 room full', 'opened 1013 room full', 'opened 1013 room full' ]`
...then after waiting 32 seconds (past the default 30-second GHOST_MS, specifically to test whether the table ever frees up): `after 32 s: new student: opened 1013 room full` -- confirming the lockout is not transient.
findings.fixSketch: Drop the `!k.snapped` condition in pruneKeys()'s eviction test (the file's own comment describing the intent -- "forget the oldest pid that is gone... and is not the instructor's" -- never mentions snapshot state at all). `left > 0 && at - k.left > GHOST_MS` already guarantees the pid has had no live connection for 30+ seconds, which is sufficient staleness regardless of whether it ever snapshotted.
findings.testSketch: Extend tests/remaining-engine.test.mjs's existing room-limit test: after filling room.keys to MAX_ROOM*2 with pids that each sent one snap and disconnected, advance the test clock past GHOST_MS and assert a brand-new pid is now accepted (today it would still get 1013).

findings.title: Binary frames are dropped before the rate limiter is ever consulted, so one connection can sustain unlimited CPU/bandwidth with zero strikes and is never disconnected
findings.where: server/relay.mjs:153
findings.scenario: `if (isBinary || !allow(ws, t, instructor ? 5 : 1)) return;` short-circuits on `isBinary` before calling `allow()`, so a binary frame never consumes a token and never increments `ws.strikes`. The file's own header comment promises "every socket has... a message rate... limit," and the equivalent-sized text traffic is in fact cut off (confirmed: a text burst gets the sender terminated after 60 messages, close code 1006), but the identical volume sent as binary frames is never limited and the socket is never closed.
findings.repro:
node /tmp/audit-scratch/relay-and-static-server-security/dyn/binflood.mjs against the unmodified relay. Printed:
`binary: sent 15485 frames of 32 KB (91 MB/s) in 5.3 s; relay CPU 28% of a core; sender still connected: true; closed code null`
`text: sent 401 small messages in a burst; connected afterwards: false; close code 1006`
-- one socket, within the room's 400-connection cap, sustaining ~91 MB/s and ~28% of one of this machine's 4 cores indefinitely with no limit and no disconnection, versus the documented and enforced behavior for text frames of the same volume.
findings.fixSketch: Call `allow()` unconditionally (it already costs nothing extra to check), then drop the frame if it is binary: `const okRate = allow(ws, t, instructor ? 5 : 1); if (!okRate) return; if (isBinary) return;` -- this keeps binary frames dropped (as intended) but makes them cost a token and count toward strikes/termination like every other frame.
findings.testSketch: Node test: open a socket, send binary frames in a tight loop past BURST, assert the socket is eventually terminated (ws.strikes exceeds 300) the same way tests/remaining-engine.test.mjs's 'Relay limits' test already asserts for a text flood.

findings.title: No SIGTERM/SIGINT handler: the relay process dies instantly on every normal deploy/restart, dropping all connections with no close frame (code 1006, not a clean close)
findings.where: server/relay.mjs:226-234 (the 'started as a program' block)
findings.scenario: The file registers `process.on('uncaughtException', ...)` and `process.on('unhandledRejection', ...)` but no `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handler at all. Node's default action for SIGTERM with no listener is immediate termination, so every connected class loses every socket as a raw TCP teardown, not a WebSocket close handshake. The README explicitly recommends deploying this on Render, Fly, or a campus VM, all of which send SIGTERM for ordinary rolling deploys and routine restarts -- meaning any ordinary deploy of a fix abruptly cuts every live classroom with zero warning to students or the instructor, and (compounding rs-seat-claim) immediately opens the exact 'room was just reset, whoever reconnects first with any role=instructor and no token wins the seat forever' window on every single restart.
findings.repro: node /tmp/audit-scratch/relay-and-static-server-security/dyn/misc1.mjs section 1 against the unmodified relay, sending SIGTERM to the spawned child while two sockets are connected. Printed: `[SIGTERM] exit {"code":null,"sig":"SIGTERM","ms":56} | client close code 1006 ""` -- the process died in 56 ms with the client seeing an unclean close (1006), not the close(1001, 'going away') a graceful shutdown would send.
findings.fixSketch: Add `for (const sig of ['SIGTERM','SIGINT']) process.on(sig, () => { for (const ws of wss.clients) ws.close(1001, 'relay restarting'); relay.close().then(() => process.exit(0)); });` in the 'started as a program' block, giving clients a real close code so js/net.js's reconnect logic (which already backs off and retries) can tell the difference between a deploy and a network drop, and giving the author a hook to log/metric restarts.
findings.testSketch: Spawn the relay as a child process, connect a socket, send SIGTERM, assert the client's close event fires with code 1001 within e.g. 500ms (today it is 1006).

findings.title: static.mjs serves a symlink's target verbatim with no realpath containment check: any symlink placed under css/js/assets/docs/dev/tests discloses arbitrary files to the whole LAN in the documented HOST=0.0.0.0 'share a lab' mode
findings.where: server/static.mjs:35-37
findings.scenario: `const full = join(root, r.file); if (full !== root && !full.startsWith(root + sep)) {...}; const data = await readFile(full);` is a plain string-prefix check on the joined path; it never calls realpath, so if `full` is itself a symlink, Node's readFile follows it to wherever it points, on or off the project, and the content is served with the extension-derived content-type. The file's own header comment promises this server "serves the app and nothing else," but that promise has no enforcement against a symlink. The scenario the file explicitly supports -- `HOST=0.0.0.0` "to share a lab" -- is exactly the case where this matters: any other account or process on that lab machine that can place a symlink under one of the six served directories (a careless `ln -s`, a compromised dependency's postinstall script touching the checkout, a shared multi-user grading server) turns the server into an arbitrary-file-read oracle for every other device on that LAN.
findings.repro: Verified without touching the shared worktree: copied server/static.mjs byte-for-byte (sha256 f9db40e3...ade11 on both the worktree file and the copy) into a scratch directory laid out the same way (index.html, assets/, css/, js/, server/), created `assets/leak.png` as a symlink to a file outside that scratch tree (`/tmp/audit-scratch/.../outside-secret.txt`, containing a timestamped marker), and ran the unmodified copy. `curl -D - http://127.0.0.1:8080/assets/leak.png` returned `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` / `content-type: image/png` with the body `TOP-SECRET-OUTSIDE-THE-SERVED-TREE-1793296580` -- the exact content of the file outside the served tree, served under a `.png` content-type because the symlink's own name has that extension.
findings.fixSketch: After computing `full`, resolve it with `realpathSync(full)` and re-check the prefix against `realpathSync(root)` before reading (and treat an ENOENT from realpathSync as 404, not a crash). This is the standard fix for this exact class of static-server bug and costs one extra syscall per request.
findings.testSketch: In a scratch tree, create a symlink under one served directory pointing to a file outside the tree; assert the server returns 404 (after the fix) instead of 200 with the outside file's content.

findings.title: Every action in the Pages deploy workflow is pinned to a floating major-version tag, not a commit SHA, while the workflow holds id-token:write + pages:write — enough to deploy to the live production site
findings.where: .github/workflows/pages.yml:17-18,34-37,42,45
findings.scenario: `actions/checkout@v7`, `actions/setup-node@v7`, `actions/configure-pages@v6`, `actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5` and `actions/deploy-pages@v5` are all pinned to major-version tags, which move: whatever commit a tag currently points to is whatever code runs with this workflow's permissions. The workflow's own `permissions:` block (`contents: read, pages: write, id-token: write`) is otherwise correctly minimal, but `pages: write` + `id-token: write` together are precisely the permissions needed to publish to the live GitHub Pages site every enrolled student and instructor loads the game from -- so a tag for any one of these five actions being re-pointed (a compromised publisher account, a hijacked release, or a maintainer's compromised token on the actions side) is a direct path to serving arbitrary content to the whole user base. This is the same pattern that caused real supply-chain incidents elsewhere in the Actions ecosystem (e.g. the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files tag-hijack) and is why GitHub's own hardening guidance and tools like OpenSSF Scorecard specifically check for commit-SHA pinning.
findings.repro: Read .github/workflows/pages.yml directly: every `uses:` line names a tag (`@v7`, `@v7`, `@v6`, `@v5`, `@v5`), not a 40-character commit SHA. No secrets beyond the ambient OIDC token are referenced, which is good, but it does not offset the floating-tag exposure for the permissions actually granted.
findings.fixSketch: Pin each action to the full commit SHA of the version currently used, with the version kept in a trailing comment for readability, e.g. `uses: actions/checkout@<40-char-sha> # v7.x.x`, and add Dependabot (`github-actions` ecosystem) or Renovate so the SHAs get bumped automatically with a reviewable diff.
findings.testSketch: A CI lint step (or a one-line grep in the existing `test` job) that fails if any `.github/workflows/*.yml` `uses:` line does not match `@[0-9a-f]{40}`.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy anywhere (no meta tag in index.html, no header from static.mjs), despite the project's explicit 'no third parties' promise
findings.where: index.html:1-84 (no <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">); server/static.mjs:38 (response headers: only content-type and cache-control)
findings.scenario: docs/FACULTY_KIT.md and docs/COMPLIANCE.md both state the game makes no third-party requests, and scripts/stage.mjs's `verify()` checks this at BUILD time (no remote `/
findings.repro: grep -n -i "content-security-policy\|x-content-type" across docs/*.md, README.md, server/*.mjs and index.html in the worktree returns nothing; reading index.html head-to-toe (84 lines) confirms no CSP meta tag; reading server/static.mjs's handler() (line 38) confirms the only headers sent are content-type and cache-control.
findings.fixSketch: Add `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' ws: wss:; img-src 'self' data:; style-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'">` to index.html's head (adjusting for the inline `application/ld+json` block, which needs either a nonce/hash or `script-src-elem 'self' 'unsafe-inline'` scoped narrowly, or simply moving the JSON-LD into main.js and injecting it at runtime). Optionally also send the same policy as a header from static.mjs and from scripts/stage.mjs's servePages() for parity with what a hardened real deployment would add in front of GitHub Pages.
findings.testSketch: Extend tests/finish-site.test.mjs (which already parses index.html) to assert a CSP meta tag is present and its connect-src does not include a wildcard or any host besides 'self'/ws/wss.

Ran the real relay (server/relay.mjs with the installed ws) on local ports in 18600-18799 and measured: idle-connection room/slot exhaustion at the 200-room and 400-connection limits; pre-emptive Founder-ID binding against the real js/net.js client; fan-out bandwidth amplification; a slow/non-reading-connection memory probe against an in-process relay; cross-room CPU/latency impact of one flooding connection; client-side (Session._onMsg) cost of ingesting snapshots at scale; and SIGTERM behavior both as a normal child process and as a container's PID 1 (via unshare --pid) — all of that ran to completion with results captured in-session. Further large-scale connection/resource scripts were then stopped by a safety classifier; I did not continue that line and did not reproduce it. The remaining items (Origin handling, security response headers, CSP, the symlink-containment pattern, workflow permissions/action pinning) were completed by reading the full source of every target file, plus one small local-filesystem-only repro outside the worktree (no network, no multiple connections) for the symlink gap. Not verified: slowloris specifically (reasoned from the absence of any custom header/connection timeout in either server, not empirically timed); the real GitHub-hosted relay or Pages deployment; anything on real hardware or non-Chromium browsers (already flagged as known/unverified).

findings.title: A handful of idle, unauthenticated sockets permanently deny the whole relay or one class's room
findings.where: server/relay.mjs:118-127 (MAX_ROOMS check), :127 (MAX_ROOM check)
findings.scenario: A room is created and a room/connection slot is consumed the instant a WebSocket upgrade with a syntactically valid room/pid/key completes (server/relay.mjs:106-144) — before 'hello' or anything else is ever sent, and regardless of whether the room code is real or guessed. Nothing ages these out: pruneKeys (line 92-97) only evicts entries from the per-room `keys` table, and only as a side effect of that table being full; it does nothing to `rooms.size` or `room.clients.size`, which is what MAX_ROOMS/MAX_ROOM actually gate.
findings.repro: Ran the real relay and opened 200 WebSocket connections, each to its own never-before-seen room code, sending nothing after the handshake. All 200 opened and stayed open. A real instructor then trying to open a brand-new room for class was refused with close code 1013 'relay full'. Separately, against a fresh relay, 400 idle connections to one specific (e.g. instructor-announced) room code filled that room; a real student joining the same code was refused with 1013 'room full'. In both cases the idle sockets never triggered the rate limiter (they send nothing) and remained open indefinitely; the client's own room-code generator (js/net.js roomCode(): a 4-character code from a 24-letter alphabet, 24^4 = 331,776 possibilities) means an attacker does not even need to know a real code — guessing new codes creates new rooms just as effectively, hitting MAX_ROOMS the same way.
findings.fixSketch: Require a connection to send something meaningful (e.g. 'hello' or a first 'snap') within a short grace window or be dropped and its slot freed; separately, age out a room/connection that has sent nothing within N seconds the same way pruneKeys ages out silent pids, so `rooms.size`/`room.clients.size` reflect real participants, not just completed handshakes.
findings.testSketch: Open MAX_ROOMS idle connections to distinct new rooms (as above); assert that after a short timeout a real instructor's new-room connection succeeds (not 1013). Open MAX_ROOM idle connections to one room; assert a real student later joining succeeds.

findings.title: A classmate who has seen a student's Founder ID can pre-bind it in a new room before the student arrives, silently and durably locking the real student out
findings.where: server/relay.mjs:128-135 (first-use binding), :1-13 (the comment claiming this is prevented); js/net.js:38-43 (RelayTransport.onclose silently retries forever)
findings.scenario: A Founder ID (pid) is sent in clear text in every relayed message by design ('every classmate knows everyone's'), and a student's browser reuses the same pid/key across every room it ever joins (js/session.js _loadIdentity). The relay's identity binding is pure trust-on-first-use per room (server/relay.mjs:130-135: whoever connects first with a given pid in a given room binds it to their key; relay.mjs's own header comment at lines 11-13 says this 'stops a classmate from taking... a classmate's name and snapshot, by connecting with the pid they have read off the wire' — but that guarantee only holds if the real owner connects first. If a classmate who merely saw the pid in an earlier class connects to a brand-new room with that pid and their own key before the real student joins, the binding goes to the classmate. When the real student's browser then tries to join with its correct, long-standing key, the relay (correctly, by its own rule) refuses the connection with close code 1008 'identity does not match' — but js/net.js's RelayTransport treats every close, including 1008, identically to a dropped network connection: it silently retries forever with exponential backoff (onclose sets state 'reconnecting' and calls open() again), and nothing in Session or the UI ever distinguishes this from an ordinary reconnect, so the student sees an app that never finishes connecting, with no error telling them why.
findings.repro: Ran the real relay and a real js/net.js Room instance (the actual production client). Opened a room, had a second connection bind the victim's pid+a different key first, then started the victim's real Room with its own (different, legitimate) key. Over 7+ seconds the victim's Room cycled 'open' -> 'reconnecting' repeatedly (the WS handshake completes, then the server immediately sends 1008 and closes), transport.tries climbed each time, and the client never reached a stable open state and never surfaced any error. The binding persists for the life of the room object (until it has had zero connected clients for EMPTY_MS = 10 minutes), so for a live class this is effectively a lockout for the whole session, not a one-off hiccup.
findings.fixSketch: Primary fix is client-side and unambiguous: RelayTransport/Room should treat close code 1008 as fatal, not transient — stop auto-retrying and surface a clear message ('this Founder ID is already in use in this room') so Session can offer a fresh identity instead of looping forever indistinguishably from a dropped connection. Separately (an author decision, not a bug): the trust-on-first-use race itself is inherent to a keyless-registration scheme and could be hardened further (e.g. only accept a pid binding from a connection within the room's first few seconds, or let the instructor pre-register expected pids), but that is a design trade-off, not what's broken here.
findings.testSketch: In js/net.js or session.js tests: simulate a relay closing with code 1008 and assert the Room/Session surfaces a distinct, user-visible state/error rather than silently scheduling another open().

findings.title: The relay's WebSocket upgrade accepts any Origin, letting any website turn a visitor's browser into a relay client
findings.where: server/relay.mjs:106-144 (the whole `connection` handler never reads req.headers.origin)
findings.scenario: The full connection handler (server/relay.mjs:106-144) parses req.url for room/pid/key/role/owner but never inspects req.headers.origin and has no allowlist of any kind. A hostile page, loaded in a visitor's browser while that visitor happens to have network access to a relay address (a LAN address in the documented HOST=0.0.0.0 lab case, or any reachable deployed relay), can open `new WebSocket('ws://<relay>/?room=<guessed-or-known-code>&pid=<any>&key=<any-16-64-char-string>&role=student')` from JavaScript it controls, with no CORS-style preflight and no same-origin restriction on WebSocket. The 16-64 char `key` requirement does stop the hostile page from impersonating a specific existing identity (it cannot read `pc.key.*` from the relay's own localStorage under the Same-Origin Policy), so this is not full account takeover — but it does let any page on the internet consume one of the 400/200 slots, read whatever that room broadcasts, and send any of the TYPES the relay accepts (snap, offer, flag, royalty, hello, etc.) as a new participant, with the request looking, to the relay, identical to a legitimate browser tab.
findings.repro: Confirmed by reading the complete 234-line file: no occurrence of `origin` (case-insensitive) anywhere in server/relay.mjs, and the ws WebSocketServer is constructed with only `{ server: http, maxPayload: MAX_MSG }` (line 71), with no `verifyClient` option set.
findings.fixSketch: Add an optional origin allowlist (e.g. ALLOWED_ORIGINS env var, checked in the `connection` handler or via WebSocketServer's verifyClient) that an operator can set when deploying the relay behind a known site; document that leaving it unset keeps today's open-to-any-origin behavior for ease of classroom setup.
findings.testSketch: Connect with a hostile Origin header set and, once ALLOWED_ORIGINS is configured, assert the upgrade is refused; assert it still succeeds with no ALLOWED_ORIGINS set (documented default) or with a matching Origin.

findings.title: The relay has no SIGTERM handler: it dies abruptly on a normal stop/redeploy, and is outright ignored when it is a container's PID 1
findings.where: server/relay.mjs:228-234 (only uncaughtException/unhandledRejection are registered; close() at :214-222 is never wired to a signal)
findings.scenario: The module exports a `close()` that cleanly terminates every connection and the HTTP/WS servers (server/relay.mjs:214-222), but nothing calls it on SIGTERM/SIGINT — only `uncaughtException` and `unhandledRejection` handlers are registered when run as a program (lines 229-231). The README documents deploying this to Render, Fly, or 'a campus VM' — all of which (and any container platform) send SIGTERM on stop/redeploy and expect the process to exit cleanly within a grace window.
findings.repro: Started the real relay with two open connections and sent it SIGTERM: the process terminated via Node's default signal action (no handler intercepted it) in well under a second, and both connected clients observed an abrupt close with code 1006 (abnormal closure), not a clean 1001 'going away' — no connection got any warning. Separately, ran the same relay as PID 1 of its own PID namespace (via `unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc`, the same situation a container's `CMD ["node", "server/relay.mjs"]` creates) and sent it SIGTERM: 1.5 seconds later the process was still alive (this is the well-known Node-as-PID-1 behavior: with no explicit handler, PID 1 does not get the kernel's default disposition for SIGTERM and the signal is simply dropped). In a container this means `docker stop`/a platform redeploy gets no clean shutdown at all and the process hangs until the platform's SIGKILL timeout, forcibly killing every connected class with zero notice on every single redeploy.
findings.fixSketch: Register `process.on('SIGTERM', ...)` and `process.on('SIGINT', ...)` that call the existing `close()` and then exit; this fixes both the bare-process case and the PID-1 case (an explicit handler is honored even as PID 1).
findings.testSketch: Spawn the relay, open a connection, send SIGTERM, and assert the client receives a clean close code (1001) before the process exits, within a short deadline.

findings.title: Chat/presence message types share the relay's full 32 KB cap with no tighter limit, so one fully legal connection's traffic is broadcast-amplified by up to ~400x bandwidth in a full room
findings.where: server/relay.mjs:155 (MAX_MSG applies uniformly to every TYPE), :172-173 (unconditional broadcast to every other client in the room)
findings.scenario: Only 'snap' has its own tighter limit (MAX_SNAP, 16 KB, relay.mjs:160); every other type (hello, bye, ack, flag, decline, reject, abort, holding, free, recall, rewound, offer, accept, confirm, deliver, royalty, clock...) is bounded only by the same 32 KB MAX_MSG that every message shares (line 155), even though none of these legitimately need more than a few hundred bytes. A single connection sending at the token-bucket's own documented legal rate (RATE=20/s) with each frame padded up toward the shared 32 KB ceiling is accepted by the rate limiter (it is well within policy) and is then broadcast, unmodified in size, to every other client in the room (lines 172-173) with no secondary cap on fan-out.
findings.repro: Ran the real relay with a full-size room of readers and one sender pushing 31 KB 'hello' frames at ~20/s (within the shipped RATE/BURST defaults the whole time; the connection never got cut off). Measured ~614 KB/s inbound from that one connection, and each of 399 simulated room members receiving ~615 KB/s, i.e. the relay's total egress for that one input stream scaled to roughly 240 MB/s with a full room — about a 399x bandwidth multiplier from one ordinary, rate-limit-compliant connection. (A related, separate observation: pushing the same load at a handful of deliberately non-reading connections did correctly trip the existing 8 MB per-connection `bufferedAmount` cutoff within about 20 seconds, self-healing the backlog — that specific safeguard is working as designed, though the transient combined backlog across many slow connections at once before they're all cut can briefly reach into the hundreds of MB.)
findings.fixSketch: Give the low-value/presence message types (hello, bye, ack, flag, decline, reject, abort, holding, free, recall, rewound, accept, confirm) their own small cap (e.g. a few hundred bytes), mirroring how 'snap' already gets MAX_SNAP instead of the full MAX_MSG.
findings.testSketch: Send a 'hello' with a large arbitrary field just under MAX_MSG; assert it is now dropped (not forwarded) once the type has its own tighter cap, while a normal small 'hello' still forwards.

findings.title: server/static.mjs's path-containment check is purely lexical: a symlink inside the served tree pointing outside the project root would be served transparently
findings.where: server/static.mjs:35-37
findings.scenario: `const full = join(root, r.file); if (full !== root && !full.startsWith(root + sep)) { ...404... }` (lines 35-36) only normalizes the path string; it never resolves the filesystem to see what `full` actually points to before `readFile(full)` (line 37) is called. `route()` already blocks `..` segments and dotfiles (line 21), so this is not reachable via ordinary path traversal — but if any file under the served directories (css/, js/, assets/, docs/, dev/, tests/) were ever a symlink whose target lies outside the project root, the lexical check would pass (the symlink's own path is inside root) while `readFile` follows the link and serves whatever is at the target, in contradiction of the file's own header comment ('It serves the app and nothing else').
findings.repro: Reproduced the exact check pattern locally (outside the worktree, no network, no server): built a 'root' directory and a sibling 'outside' directory with a secret file, placed a symlink at root/assets/favicon.svg pointing to the outside file, and ran the identical `join(root, ...)` + `startsWith(root + sep)` logic against it. The lexical check reported the path as contained (`startsWith(root+sep) === true`), while `readFileSync` returned the outside file's content and `realpathSync` showed the true resolved path does NOT start with root. No symlink currently exists in the audited tree (confirmed: a tree-wide search for symbolic links in the worktree found none), so this is a latent gap, not an active exploit today.
findings.fixSketch: After computing `full`, call `realpathSync(full)` (and `realpathSync(root)` once at startup) and require the resolved real path to still start with the real root before reading; fail closed (404) otherwise.
findings.testSketch: Create a symlink under one of the served directories pointing outside the project root in a throwaway fixture tree, request it through `handler`, and assert a 404 instead of the outside content.

findings.title: The Pages workflow grants pages:write/id-token:write to a job that never deploys, and pins third-party actions only to mutable major-version tags
findings.where: .github/workflows/pages.yml:5-9 (workflow-level permissions), :14-21 (the `test` job's steps), :15,16,27,36,38 (uses: ...@v7/@v6/@v5)
findings.scenario: `permissions: { contents: read, pages: write, id-token: write }` is declared once at the workflow level (lines 5-9), so GitHub Actions grants it to both jobs. The `test` job (lines 11-21) only runs `npm ci --prefix server` and `npm test` — it has no legitimate use for `pages: write` or the OIDC `id-token: write` token, yet holds both. If any dependency pulled in by `npm ci` (directly or transitively) were ever compromised, the `test` job's runner would carry deploy-capable credentials it does not need, which is exactly what least-privilege scoping exists to prevent. Separately, every third-party action is pinned only to a major-version tag (`actions/checkout@v7`, `setup-node@v7`, `configure-pages@v6`, `upload-pages-artifact@v5`, `deploy-pages@v5`): these tags are mutable aliases, not fixed commits, so a future retag of any of them (by its maintainer, or in a supply-chain compromise of that action's repo) would silently change what code runs in this workflow with no diff in this repository to review.
findings.repro: Read the full 45-line workflow: the `permissions:` block sits above `jobs:` with no job-level override in either `test` or `deploy`, so by GitHub Actions' documented inheritance rule both jobs get the full set. Confirmed each `uses:` line matches `^[\w.-]+/[\w.-]+@v\d+$` (a bare major-version tag, not a 40-character SHA) for all five actions used. Confirmed via `git ls-remote --tags` against each action's real repository that `v7`/`v6`/`v5` are live, currently-resolvable tags distinct from a pinned commit (e.g. actions/checkout's `v7` and `v7.0.1` tags point to the same commit today, but `v7` itself is the kind of tag that can be moved by the upstream maintainer, unlike a commit SHA).
findings.fixSketch: Move `pages: write` / `id-token: write` to the `deploy` job only (job-level `permissions:`), leaving `test` with just `contents: read`; pin each `uses:` to the full commit SHA it currently resolves to, with a trailing comment noting the version (e.g. `actions/checkout@<sha> # v7.0.1`).
findings.testSketch: Update the existing workflow test (tests/finish-site.test.mjs's 'the Pages workflow...' test, which today asserts the elevated permissions at the top level) to instead assert `jobs.test.permissions` is absent/minimal and the elevated grants live only on `jobs.deploy`; add an assertion that every `uses:` value matches a 40-character SHA.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy on the deployed page and no X-Content-Type-Options on the local dev server's responses
findings.where: index.html:1-66 (head, no CSP meta); server/static.mjs:38 (only content-type and cache-control are set); scripts/stage.mjs:237 (servePages sets the same two headers plus CORS, no nosniff/CSP)
findings.scenario: GitHub Pages does not let a static site set arbitrary HTTP response headers, so the only way this project could ever ship a CSP on the real deployed site is a `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` tag in index.html; none exists (confirmed by reading the full 84-line file). `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` cannot be set via `<meta>` at all, so it is unreachable on the real Pages deployment regardless — but the local dev server (server/static.mjs, used for `npm start` and for every headless-Chrome test run) and its Pages-mimic (scripts/stage.mjs's `servePages`, used by `npm run preview`) are both under this project's own control and also omit it (both set only `content-type`/`cache-control`, servePages additionally sets `access-control-allow-origin: '*'` and `vary`, but never `x-content-type-options`).
findings.repro: Confirmed by reading both complete files: server/static.mjs's only `writeHead` header object (line 38) is `{ 'content-type': ..., 'cache-control': 'no-store' }`; scripts/stage.mjs's `servePages` header object (line 237) adds only `content-length`, `cache-control`, `access-control-allow-origin`, `vary`, and conditionally `content-encoding`/`location` — `x-content-type-options` appears in neither file, and no occurrence of `Content-Security-Policy` exists anywhere in index.html.
findings.fixSketch: Add a CSP `<meta>` tag to index.html scoped to what the page actually needs (no inline scripts are used today, so a fairly strict `default-src 'self'` policy should fit); add `x-content-type-options: nosniff` to the header object in both server/static.mjs's `handler` and scripts/stage.mjs's `servePages`.
findings.testSketch: Assert index.html contains a CSP meta tag; assert a response from `handler`/`servePages` includes `x-content-type-options: nosniff`.
